title: Short Stuff: Tooth Fairy: Not Real
summary: Josh and Chuck discuss the tooth fairy as a Short Stuff episode. They cover Josh's daughter's first lost tooth and the money question, then the tooth fairy's recent American origins (early mentions in 1908 and 1927 and the 1949 Collier's article), the history of tooth-disposal rituals around the world (mice and rats, throwing teeth onto roofs or into fires, burial links, and swallowing a tooth), the likely influence of Disney fairy films, the Norse tooth fee, the modern going rate of about $3.70 median, and parents teaching kids about money. The episode ends with a Janet Varney shout-out and a sign-off.

segments.title: Opening banter and the tooth fairy's origins
segments.summary: Josh introduces the episode and explains that his daughter has not yet lost a tooth. The hosts joke about how much money kids get, and Josh recalls getting a quarter for giving up his pacifier. They note the tooth fairy is a relatively young American figure, with early references in the 1908 Chicago Daily Tribune and a 1927 play, and a 1920s mouse-tooth-fairy book, before the Collier's article in May 1949 spread the tradition.

segments.title: Tooth-related rituals around the world
segments.summary: The hosts describe tooth traditions in countries such as Afghanistan, Russia, Mexico and New Zealand, many involving a mouse or rat so the child's tooth grows back strong. They mention sympathetic magic, a list of disposal rituals (throwing the tooth onto a roof, into a fire, or the sun), links to burial customs, and a practice in which a parent or child has an animal swallow the tooth as a rite of passage.

segments.title: How the modern tooth fairy and tooth money came about
segments.summary: The hosts connect the American tooth fairy to Disney fairy films such as Pinocchio and Cinderella from the same period. They say the payment for teeth dates back to a twelfth-century Norse custom of paying a tooth fee. They give a median going rate of about $3.70, noting that the average is pulled up by parents who pay more, and discuss using the tooth as a lesson in money.

segments.title: Teaching kids money and closing chat
segments.summary: Josh says a folklore explanation ties the American tooth fairy to teaching kids about exchange and capitalism. He mentions his daughter's piggy banks and his plan to show her the value of a tooth. The hosts then mention their own fake teeth and joke about what they could get for them.

segments.title: Janet Varney shout-out and sign-off
segments.summary: Josh gives a shout-out to podcaster Janet Varney and mentions the tooth fairy pillow she sent him after he appeared on her JV Club Live show. The episode closes with the standard sign-off and the iHeartRadio credit.
